title: GitHub OAuth App for an agent that reads repos, issues and PRs and opens PRs
useCase: An AI agent that, on behalf of a signed-in GitHub user, lists and reads their repositories, issues and pull requests, and creates branches/commits/pull requests. Built on a classic OAuth App (user-scoped tokens), not a GitHub App.
audience: Solo developer or small startup building an agent product; comfortable implementing the OAuth web flow and REST/GraphQL calls.
assumptions: You register your own OAuth App under your personal account or an org you administer; no managed/third-party app.
Users authorize via the standard web application flow (device flow optional for CLI/headless agents).
The agent needs write access to private repos (to open PRs), which is why the broad `repo` scope is required on an OAuth App.

OAuth App vs GitHub App: pick an OAuth App when you want the simplest setup and act strictly as the user (the PR is authored by them). Pick a GitHub App when users should limit you to specific repos, you want issues/PR access without repo contents, you need a bot identity, or you expect to scale API volume. GitHub itself says GitHub Apps are preferred. Steps below are for the OAuth App.

registration.summary: Any GitHub user can register an OAuth App immediately under their personal account or any organization they administer (up to 100 apps per owner). Registration is a form; the docs describe no GitHub review or approval step before the app can be authorized by other users.

scopes.name: repo
scopes.purpose: Required to read private repositories and to push branches and open PRs. Broad: full read/write to code, commit statuses, invitations, collaborators, deployment statuses and repo webhooks on every public and private repo the user can reach. An OAuth App cannot request anything narrower for private-repo contents; `public_repo` covers public repos only.

scopes.name: read:user
scopes.purpose: Read the user's profile data (login, name, avatar) to identify the signed-in account.

scopes.name: user:email
scopes.purpose: Read the user's email addresses (including private ones) for account linking/notifications.

difficulty.rationale: No provider review, no verification, no quotas on user count. The work is the standard OAuth code flow plus handling expiring tokens (8h access / 6-month refresh, on by default for new apps). The main real-world friction is not GitHub review but organization OAuth app access restrictions (on by default for new orgs), which silently strip the token's access to org repos until an org owner approves your app.

handsOnEffort.basis: Registration form takes minutes; most time goes to implementing the authorization code exchange, refresh-token rotation, and a UX path telling users to request org approval. Longer if you add device flow for a CLI agent.

providerWait.basis: No GitHub review exists for OAuth Apps, so there is no provider wait to publish. Org-owner approval under access restrictions is at each org's discretion and has no published SLA.

reviewStages.name: GitHub app review / approval
reviewStages.trigger: Never for a plain OAuth App: the registration docs end at 'Register application' with no review step.

reviewStages.name: Organization owner approval (OAuth app access policy)
reviewStages.trigger: A user authorizes your app and wants it to touch repos of an org that has OAuth app access restrictions enabled (default for new orgs). Members request; an org owner grants or denies. Per org, not per app globally.

reviewStages.name: GitHub Marketplace listing verification
reviewStages.trigger: Only if you choose to list on Marketplace. Free listings need the general requirements; paid plans need an org that is a verified publisher and, for OAuth apps, a minimum of 200 users. Not needed to distribute the app.

prerequisites: A GitHub account (personal, or org you administer if the app should be org-owned from day one).
A public homepage URL for the app.
An HTTPS callback URL for production; a loopback (127.0.0.1 / ::1) URL for local dev.
Server-side secret storage for the client secret (web flow). Device flow needs no secret.
artifacts: Client ID (public) and client secret (generated after registration, store server-side)
Optional: application description and logo shown on the consent screen
User-facing instructions for requesting org approval when a token lacks org repo access

steps.title: Register the OAuth App
steps.details: Profile → Settings → Developer settings → OAuth apps → New OAuth App. Fill Application name, Homepage URL, optional description, Authorization callback URL. Decide the owner now (personal vs org); it can be transferred later. Treat everything on the form as public.
steps.ownerNote: Requires an authenticated GitHub session (and 2FA if enabled on the account).

steps.title: Configure callback URLs, device flow, token expiry
steps.details: Add every redirect you will use (prod HTTPS, staging, loopback for dev; up to 10). Redirect URI must exactly match a registered callback unless you enable wildcard matching (GitHub warns this adds risk). Loopback redirects may use any port. Tick 'Enable Device Flow' only if your agent runs headless/CLI. 'Expire user access tokens' is on by default; leave it on and implement refresh.

steps.title: Generate and store the client secret
steps.details: On the app page click 'Generate a new client secret'. Store it in a secrets manager or encrypted env var. Never ship it in a browser/mobile/CLI build; those are public clients and should use device flow or PKCE.
steps.ownerNote: Secret is displayed once in the browser session; a human must copy it into the secret store.

steps.title: Implement the web application flow
steps.details: Redirect to https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=…&redirect_uri=…&scope=repo%20read:user%20user:email&state=…. Exchange the returned code at https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token within 10 minutes. Check `expires_in` in the response to know you got an expiring token; persist access + refresh tokens per user.

steps.title: Implement refresh-token rotation
steps.details: Access tokens expire after 8 hours, refresh tokens after 6 months of non-use. Each refresh invalidates the old access and refresh token, so write the new pair atomically before using it. Scopes are not re-prompted on refresh.

steps.title: (Optional) Implement device flow for a CLI agent
steps.details: POST https://github.com/login/device/code with client_id and scope; show user_code + verification_uri; poll https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token with grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code honoring `interval` (back off 5s on `slow_down`). Code valid 15 minutes. No client secret needed. 50 code submissions/hour/app limit.

steps.title: Handle reduced scopes and org access restrictions
steps.details: Users can edit requested scopes on the consent screen, so read the `X-OAuth-Scopes` header and degrade gracefully. If a user's org has OAuth app access restrictions on (default for new orgs), the token cannot see that org's repos until an org owner approves the app; show instructions: Settings → Applications → Authorized OAuth Apps → your app → Request access → Request approval from owners. Org owners approve at Org Settings → Third-party Access → OAuth app policy.

steps.title: Test with your own account and budget rate limits
steps.details: Authorize with your own account; list repos, read issues/PRs, push a branch and open a PR on a scratch repo. Plan for 5,000 requests/hour per user (shared with any other OAuth app/PAT the user uses) and no scaling; use conditional requests and GraphQL batching. Secondary limit: 2,000 token requests/hour per app.

steps.title: (Optional) Transfer the app to an organization
steps.details: Settings → Developer settings → OAuth apps → app → Transfer ownership; type the app name and the new owner's username/org. The recipient must open their OAuth apps page under 'Pending transfer requests' and click Complete transfer. Do this before Marketplace listing (org ownership required).
steps.ownerNote: Both sender and recipient must act in the GitHub UI; recipient confirmation is a consent step.

steps.title: (Optional) List on GitHub Marketplace
steps.details: Only org owners can create/submit listings. Free plan: meet the general listing requirements and request verification of the listing. Paid plans: org must be a verified publisher, OAuth apps need ≥200 users, plus billing webhook handling and financial onboarding. Not needed to distribute; any user can authorize your app without a listing.
steps.ownerNote: Involves accepting the Marketplace Developer Agreement and publisher verification (legal/financial representations).

availableNow: Full OAuth web flow and device flow against your own account immediately after registration.
Any other GitHub user can authorize the app right away; no tester allowlist or app-review gate.
Real API calls at the normal 5,000 req/hour user limit; no sandbox tier.
restrictions: Tokens for users in orgs with OAuth app access restrictions enabled will not see those org repos until an owner approves the app.
Users may deselect scopes at consent, so test the reduced-scope path.
Device flow is rejected with device_flow_disabled unless enabled in app settings; 50 verification-code submissions/hour/app.
Enterprise managed users: docs confirm they can create OAuth apps and restrict GitHub App installs; their ability to authorize third-party OAuth apps was not explicitly stated on the fetched page.

requirements: Registered OAuth App with production callback URL and client secret stored server-side.
Refresh-token rotation implemented (expiring tokens are the default).
UX for reduced scopes and for org-approval requests.
No GitHub review, verification, or Marketplace listing required to let arbitrary users authorize.

blockers.title: Token works but org repos are invisible / PR creation 404s
blockers.description: The user's organization has OAuth app access restrictions enabled (default for new orgs). Your app loses access to that org's resources until an owner approves it, even though the user granted `repo`.
blockers.recovery: Have the user request approval (Settings → Applications → Authorized OAuth Apps → app → Request access → Request approval from owners) and an org owner grant it under Org Settings → Third-party Access → OAuth app policy. If the org refuses OAuth apps on policy grounds, offer a GitHub App instead.

blockers.title: redirect_uri mismatch
blockers.description: Redirect must exactly match a registered callback URL unless wildcard matching is enabled; the only relaxation is that loopback redirects may use any port.
blockers.recovery: Register each exact URL (up to 10). For local dev use http://127.0.0.1:<any-port>/callback with a registered 127.0.0.1 callback. Avoid wildcard matching unless needed.

blockers.title: Access token suddenly unauthorized after ~8 hours
blockers.description: New apps issue expiring tokens by default; the access token dies after eight hours and refresh tokens after six months without use. Using a refresh token invalidates the previous pair.
blockers.recovery: Implement refresh before expiry (track `expires_in`), store the new pair atomically, and re-run the auth flow if the refresh token is gone. Do not turn off expiry just to avoid the work.

blockers.title: Rate limit exhaustion for heavy agent loops
blockers.description: OAuth tokens draw on the user's 5,000 req/hour budget shared with every other OAuth app and PAT they use, and OAuth app limits do not scale with repos/users.
blockers.recovery: Use conditional requests (ETag), GraphQL to batch, cache repo metadata, and back off on 403/429 with `x-ratelimit-reset`. If volume is the bottleneck, migrate to a GitHub App whose installation limits scale.

blockers.title: User granted fewer scopes than requested
blockers.description: On the consent screen users can edit scopes, granting less than you asked for; the token may lack `repo`.
blockers.recovery: Read `X-OAuth-Scopes` on any response, explain which features are disabled, and offer to re-run the authorize URL; the user may still decline.

blockers.title: Leaked client secret
blockers.description: Client secret is required for the web flow token exchange; if it ships in a public client or leaks it must be rotated.
blockers.recovery: Generate a new secret on the app page, deploy it, then delete the old one. Move public clients to device flow or PKCE.

nextActions: Register the OAuth App now; nothing gates it.
Implement authorize → code exchange → refresh rotation with `repo read:user user:email`.
Build the 'request org approval' UX before onboarding anyone in an organization.
Decide early whether a GitHub App is the better long-term fit (repo-scoped install, bot identity, scaling rate limits).

claims.text: An OAuth App can be registered under a personal account or any organization the user administers; an owner may have up to 100 OAuth apps.
claims.excerpt: under your personal account or under any organization you have administrative access to. ... A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

claims.text: There is no GitHub review or approval step to publish an OAuth App; the registration procedure ends with clicking Register application.
claims.excerpt: Final documented step is "Click Register application." The page contains no statement about any review or approval process; absence of a documented step, not an explicit 'no review' statement.

claims.text: Up to 10 authorization callback URLs can be registered per OAuth App.
claims.excerpt: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs. To add additional callback URLs, click Add callback URL.

claims.text: Device flow must be enabled in app settings, needs no client secret, user codes expire after 15 minutes, and there is a 50 submissions/hour/app limit.
claims.excerpt: you must first enable it in your app's settings. ... The client_secret is not needed for the device flow. ... The user must enter a valid code within 15 minutes (or 900 seconds). ... there is a rate limit of 50 submissions in an hour per application

claims.text: Loopback redirect URIs are allowed and need not match the port in the registered callback; GitHub points to the RFC recommendation of 127.0.0.1 / ::1 over localhost.
claims.excerpt: The redirect_uri does not need to match the port specified in the callback URL for the app. ... recommends not to use localhost, but instead to use loopback literal 127.0.0.1 or IPv6 ::1

claims.text: Without wildcard matching the redirect_uri must exactly match a registered callback URL; wildcard matching is available but flagged as a security risk.
claims.excerpt: When wildcard matching is disabled, the redirect URL must exactly match the callback URL. ... can expose your app to security risks.

claims.text: Expiring user tokens are enabled by default for new OAuth Apps: access tokens expire after eight hours, refresh tokens after six months without use; using a refresh token invalidates the old pair.
claims.excerpt: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use. ... Once you use a refresh token, that refresh token and the old access token will no longer work. (Creating page: "Expire user access tokens is enabled by default.")

claims.text: The repo scope grants full read/write access to all public and private repositories the user can access, including code, commit statuses, invitations, collaborators, deployment statuses and webhooks.
claims.excerpt: Grants full access to public and private repositories including read and write access to code, commit statuses,

claims.text: read:user grants read access to profile data; user:email grants read access to the user's email addresses.
claims.excerpt: Grants access to read a user's profile data. ... Grants read access to a user's email addresses.

claims.text: Users can edit requested scopes at consent time, granting less than requested; scopes never exceed the user's own permissions.
claims.excerpt: users can edit their scopes, effectively granting your application less access than you originally requested. ... do not grant any additional permission beyond that which the user already has.

claims.text: GitHub recommends GitHub Apps over OAuth Apps; OAuth Apps cannot use granular permissions and are limited via scopes, whereas an authorized OAuth App can access everything the user can.
claims.excerpt: In general, GitHub Apps are preferred to OAuth apps ... OAuth apps can't use granular permissions. ... An OAuth access token is limited via scopes.

claims.text: OAuth tokens use the user's primary rate limit of 5,000 requests/hour (shared across the user's apps/PATs) and OAuth app limits do not scale.
claims.excerpt: All of these requests count towards your personal rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour. (Differences page: "OAuth tokens use the user's rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour." and "OAuth apps have lower rate limits and do not scale.")

claims.text: Secondary limit: no more than 2,000 OAuth access token requests per hour per app.
claims.excerpt: No more than 2,000 OAuth access token requests per hour are allowed for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps.

claims.text: OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default for new organizations; when enabled, OAuth apps lose access to the org's resources and members must request owner approval.
claims.excerpt: When you create a new organization, OAuth app access restrictions are enabled by default. ... OAuth apps immediately lose access to the organization's resources.

claims.text: A user requests org approval from Settings → Applications → Authorized OAuth Apps → app → Request access → Request approval from owners; organization owners approve or deny under Third-party Access → OAuth app policy.
claims.excerpt: click the name of the OAuth app you'd like to request access for. ... click Request access. ... click Request approval from owners. (Approving page: "organization owners can approve or deny the request.")

claims.text: OAuth App ownership can be transferred to another user or organization; the transfer completes only when the recipient clicks Complete transfer.
claims.excerpt: You can transfer ownership of an OAuth app to another user or organization. ... the new owner needs to navigate to their OAuth apps page ... click Complete transfer.

claims.text: Marketplace listing is optional; only org owners can submit listings; paid plans require a verified-publisher org and OAuth apps need at least 200 users; free listings need only the general requirements.
claims.excerpt: only organization owners can create and submit listings in GitHub Marketplace. ... your app must be owned by an organization that is a verified publisher. ... OAuth apps should have a minimum of 200 users.

claims.text: Enterprise managed user accounts can create OAuth apps and GitHub Apps, but cannot install GitHub Apps on their user accounts unless the app is privileged.
claims.excerpt: Can create GitHub Apps and OAuth apps. ... Cannot install GitHub Apps on their user accounts, unless the app is an privileged app.

claims.text: Client secrets are required for token generation except with device flow; public clients cannot protect the secret and should use PKCE; a compromised secret must be regenerated and the old one deleted.
claims.excerpt: Client secrets are required to generate access tokens for your app, unless your app uses the device flow. ... you should use PKCE to better secure the authentication flow. ... generate a new secret, update your app to use the new secret, and delete your old secret.

claims.text: Immediately after registration any GitHub user can authorize the OAuth App; there is no tester allowlist, user cap, or unverified-app warning for OAuth Apps.
claims.excerpt: Inferred from the absence of any review, allowlist or cap in the creating/authorizing docs (c2). No page fetched states this explicitly.

claims.text: Apps owned by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization get a higher 15,000 requests/hour limit for requests on a user's behalf.
claims.excerpt: have a higher rate limit of 15,000 requests per hour.

claims.text: The temporary authorization code from the web flow expires after 10 minutes.
claims.excerpt: The temporary code will expire after 10 minutes.

unresolved: No page states explicitly 'OAuth Apps are not reviewed'; the conclusion rests on the absence of any review step in the docs.
